claim: Drosophila neuroblasts express opposing temporal gradients of RNA-binding proteins, Imp and Syp.
source: First, Drosophila neuroblasts express opposing temporal gradients of RNA-binding proteins, Imp and Syp.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Imp and Syp promote or inhibit chinmo translation, yielding a descending neuronal gradient.
source: These proteins promote or inhibit chinmo translation, yielding a descending neuronal gradient.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: First and second-layer temporal factors define a temporal expression window of BTB-zinc finger nuclear protein, Mamo.
source: Together, first and second-layer temporal factors define a temporal expression window of BTB-zinc finger nuclear protein, Mamo.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a key finding.

claim: The precise temporal induction of Mamo is achieved via both transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation.
source: The precise temporal induction of Mamo is achieved via both transcriptional and post-transcriptional regulation.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by smFISH and immunostaining data.

claim: Mamo is essential for the temporally defined, terminal identity of α'/β' mushroom body neurons.
source: Finally, Mamo is essential for the temporally defined, terminal identity of α'/β' mushroom body neurons and identity maintenance.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by loss-of-function and gain-of-function experiments.

claim: Mamo is essential for identity maintenance of α'/β' mushroom body neurons.
source: Finally, Mamo is essential for the temporally defined, terminal identity of α'/β' mushroom body neurons and identity maintenance.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract and supported by adult-specific RNAi experiments.

claim: Orthologous/related mammalian genes suggest a fundamental conservation of this mechanism in brain development.
source: The neurodevelopmental roles of orthologous/related mammalian genes suggest a fundamental conservation of this mechanism in brain development.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and discussed in the manuscript based on literature citations.

claim: In the mouse neocortex, radial glial progenitors are multipotent and produce a variety of neuron types organized sequentially into six layers, and then produce glia.
source: For example, in the mouse neocortex, radial glial progenitors (RGP) are multipotent—they produce a variety of neuron types organized sequentially into six layers, and then produce glia (Adnani et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: An individual neurogenic radial glial progenitor produces an average of 8–9 progeny (range of 3–16) that can span all cortical layers.
source: In vivo lineage analysis demonstrated that after a stage of symmetric cell division, an individual neurogenic RGP produces an average of 8–9 progeny (range of 3–16) that can span all cortical layers (Gao et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Clonal analysis in Drosophila has demonstrated a vast range of stem cell-specific lineage programs.
source: In Drosophila, clonal analysis has demonstrated a vast range of stem cell-specific lineage programs (Ito et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Lineage tracing of a single antennal lobe stem cell revealed a remarkable series of 40 morphologically distinct neuronal types generated sequentially.
source: On one extreme, lineage tracing of a single antennal lobe (AL) stem cell revealed a remarkable series of 40 morphologically distinct neuronal types generated sequentially (Lin et al., 2012; Yu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Many temporal transcription factors originally discovered in the fly have since been confirmed to have conserved roles in mouse retinal and cortical development.
source: Many temporal transcription factors originally discovered in the fly have since been confirmed to have conserved roles in mouse retinal and cortical development (Holguera and Desplan, 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Temporal expression of Imp guides temporal patterning in the postembryonic fly brain.
source: Moreover, temporal expression of an RNA binding protein, IGF-II mRNA-binding protein (Imp), that guides temporal patterning in the postembryonic fly brain (Liu et al., 2015) is also implicated in mouse brain development (Nishino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Temporal expression of Imp is implicated in mouse brain development.
source: Moreover, temporal expression of an RNA binding protein, IGF-II mRNA-binding protein (Imp), that guides temporal patterning in the postembryonic fly brain (Liu et al., 2015) is also implicated in mouse brain development (Nishino et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: In the embryonic ventral nerve cord and the optic lobe, neuroblasts express a rapidly changing series of four to six temporal transcription factors.
source: In the embryonic ventral nerve cord and the optic lobe, the NBs express a rapidly changing series of four to six temporal transcription factors (tTF), some of which are directly inherited by the daughter neurons (Baumgardt et al., 2009; Isshiki et al., 2001; Kanai et al., 2005; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Some temporal transcription factors are directly inherited by the daughter neurons.
source: In the embryonic ventral nerve cord and the optic lobe, the NBs express a rapidly changing series of four to six temporal transcription factors (tTF), some of which are directly inherited by the daughter neurons (Baumgardt et al., 2009; Isshiki et al., 2001; Kanai et al., 2005; Li et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Each temporal transcription factor directly acts to specify a small number (two to four) of neuronal progeny.
source: Each tTF directly acts to specify a small number (two to four) of neuronal progeny.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Imp and Syp control neuronal temporal fate specification.
source: These proteins are Imp and Syncrip (Syp) RNA-binding proteins. Imp and Syp control neuronal temporal fate specification as well as the timing of NB termination (decommissioning; Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Imp and Syp control the timing of neuroblast termination (decommissioning).
source: These proteins are Imp and Syncrip (Syp) RNA-binding proteins. Imp and Syp control neuronal temporal fate specification as well as the timing of NB termination (decommissioning; Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017; Yang et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Imp promotes chinmo translation.
source: Imp promotes and Syp inhibits translation of the BTB-zinc finger nuclear protein, chinmo (chronologically inappropriate morphogenesis), so that protein levels in newborn neurons descend over time (Figure 1A) (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Syp inhibits chinmo translation.
source: Imp promotes and Syp inhibits translation of the BTB-zinc finger nuclear protein, chinmo (chronologically inappropriate morphogenesis), so that protein levels in newborn neurons descend over time (Figure 1A) (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and reference to Figure 1A.

claim: Chinmo protein levels in newborn neurons descend over time.
source: Imp promotes and Syp inhibits translation of the BTB-zinc finger nuclear protein, chinmo (chronologically inappropriate morphogenesis), so that protein levels in newborn neurons descend over time (Figure 1A) (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation and shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The level of Chinmo correlates with the specification of multiple neuronal temporal fates.
source: The level of Chinmo correlates with the specification of multiple neuronal temporal fates (Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mushroom body neuronal lineages are comprised of only three major cell types.
source: Temporal regulation in the fly brain is easily studied in the relatively simple mushroom body (MB) neuronal lineages which are comprised of only three major cell types.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on established knowledge.

claim: Mushroom body neuronal types are born in sequential order: beginning with γ neurons, followed by α'/β' neurons, and finally α/β neurons.
source: These neuronal types are born in sequential order: beginning with γ neurons, followed by α'/β' neurons, and finally α/β neurons (Ito et al., 1997; Lee et al., 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to support the claim.

claim: Imp and Syp are expressed in relatively shallow, opposing temporal gradients in the mushroom body neuroblasts.
source: Imp and Syp are expressed in relatively shallow, opposing temporal gradients in the MB NBs.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on prior work.

claim: Modulation of Imp or Syp expression results in shifts in the neuronal temporal fate.
source: Modulation of Imp or Syp expression results in shifts in the neuronal temporal fate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on prior work.

claim: Imp and Syp post-transcriptionally control Chinmo so that it is expressed in a gradient in the first two temporal windows.
source: Imp and Syp post-transcriptionally control Chinmo so that it is expressed in a gradient in the first two temporal windows (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: γ neurons are produced in a high Chinmo window.
source: γ neurons are produced in a high Chinmo window, α'/β' neurons are produced in a low Chinmo window, and α/β neurons are produced in a window absent of Chinmo expression (Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: α'/β' neurons are produced in a low Chinmo window.
source: γ neurons are produced in a high Chinmo window, α'/β' neurons are produced in a low Chinmo window, and α/β neurons are produced in a window absent of Chinmo expression (Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: α/β neurons are produced in a window absent of Chinmo expression.
source: γ neurons are produced in a high Chinmo window, α'/β' neurons are produced in a low Chinmo window, and α/β neurons are produced in a window absent of Chinmo expression (Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Altering Chinmo levels can shift the temporal fate of mushroom body neurons.
source: Moreover, altering Chinmo levels can shift the temporal fate of MB neurons accordingly, strongly implicating dose-dependent actions, similar to that of a morphogen.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction based on prior work.

claim: Chinmo has dose-dependent actions, similar to that of a morphogen.
source: Moreover, altering Chinmo levels can shift the temporal fate of MB neurons accordingly, strongly implicating dose-dependent actions, similar to that of a morphogen.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as an inference from experimental observations.

claim: Mamo is a BTB zinc finger transcription factor critical for temporal specification of α'/β' neurons.
source: Here we describe Mamo (maternal gene required for meiosis, Mukai et al., 2007), a BTB zinc finger transcription factor critical for temporal specification of α'/β' neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a primary finding of the study.

claim: Mamo is expressed in a low Chinmo temporal window.
source: Mamo is expressed in a low Chinmo temporal window and Mamo expression can be inhibited both by high Chinmo levels and loss of chinmo.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Mamo expression can be inhibited both by high Chinmo levels and loss of chinmo.
source: Mamo is expressed in a low Chinmo temporal window and Mamo expression can be inhibited both by high Chinmo levels and loss of chinmo.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Mamo is post-transcriptionally regulated by the Syp RNA binding protein.
source: Additionally, Mamo is post-transcriptionally regulated by the Syp RNA binding protein.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Layered regulation of Mamo is utilized in both mushroom body and antennal lobe lineages.
source: This layered regulation, which is utilized in both MB and AL lineages results in a discrete window of Mamo expression in young, post-mitotic neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Layered regulation results in a discrete window of Mamo expression in young, post-mitotic neurons.
source: This layered regulation, which is utilized in both MB and AL lineages results in a discrete window of Mamo expression in young, post-mitotic neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: The window of Mamo expression corresponds to the middle window of neurogenesis in mushroom body lineages.
source: In the MB lineages, this window corresponds to the middle window of neurogenesis and we establish that Mamo codes for middle temporal fate(s); α'/β' neuronal characteristics are lost when Mamo levels are reduced and ectopic Mamo drives an increase in α'/β' neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: α'/β' neuronal characteristics are lost when Mamo levels are reduced.
source: In the MB lineages, this window corresponds to the middle window of neurogenesis and we establish that Mamo codes for middle temporal fate(s); α'/β' neuronal characteristics are lost when Mamo levels are reduced and ectopic Mamo drives an increase in α'/β' neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Ectopic Mamo drives an increase in α'/β' neuron production.
source: In the MB lineages, this window corresponds to the middle window of neurogenesis and we establish that Mamo codes for middle temporal fate(s); α'/β' neuronal characteristics are lost when Mamo levels are reduced and ectopic Mamo drives an increase in α'/β' neuron production.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a finding of the study.

claim: Mamo deciphers the upstream temporal specification code and acts as a terminal selector to determine neuronal fate.
source: Our data suggest that Mamo deciphers the upstream temporal specification code and acts as a terminal selector to determine neuronal fate.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from the study.

claim: Mamo expression seems to trail weak Chinmo expression in both time and space.
source: Mamo expression seems to trail weak Chinmo expression in both time and space (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B-D.

claim: α'/β' neurons are specified in a temporal window when Chinmo levels in newborn neurons are weak, beginning around 72 hr after larval hatching.
source: α'/β' neurons are specified in a temporal window when Chinmo levels in newborn neurons are weak, beginning around 72 hr after larval hatching (h ALH) (Zhu et al., 2006) (Figure 1B, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and supported by Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mamo's expression is initiated around 84 hr after larval hatching in a group of neurons that border the newborn neurons.
source: Mamo's expression is initiated a few hours afterwards (around 84 hr ALH) in a group of neurons that border the newborn neurons (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Mamo is undetectable in young/maturing neurons that are destined to become γ or α/β neurons.
source: Conversely, Mamo is undetectable in young/maturing neurons that are destined to become γ (Figure 1B) or α/β neurons (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1B and 1D.

claim: At 84 hr ALH, Mamo is expressed in prospective α'/β' rather than γ neurons.
source: To validate that at 84 hr ALH, Mamo is in fact expressed in prospective α'/β' rather than γ neurons, we used a γ neuron-specific driver and confirmed that there is no overlap with Mamo expression (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: γ neurons begin to express Mamo during puparium formation.
source: γ neurons, which express high Chinmo in early larval stages, begin to express Mamo during puparium formation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Both overexpressing and eliminating Chinmo effectively abolished Mamo expression.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, both overexpressing and eliminating Chinmo effectively abolished Mamo expression (Figure 2B and C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2B, 2C, and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Chinmo's effect on Mamo expression appears to be cell autonomous.
source: Chinmo's effect on Mamo expression appears to be cell autonomous, as wild type neurons adjacent to chinmo null MARCM clones continue to express Mamo (Figure 2C, yellow arrow).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2C.

claim: Targeted chinmo RNAi prematurely reduced, rather than eliminating Chinmo.
source: Conversely, targeted chinmo RNAi prematurely reduced, rather than eliminating Chinmo (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B&G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and G.

claim: Premature reduction in Chinmo initiated early Mamo expression.
source: This premature reduction in Chinmo initiated early Mamo expression (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B) and thus greatly expanded (approximately 3-fold) the number of cells expressing Mamo at 84 hr ALH (Figure 2D and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 2D, and Figure 2G.

claim: Weak Chinmo expression is both necessary and sufficient to activate Mamo in young/maturing mushroom body neurons.
source: These results indicate that weak Chinmo expression is both necessary and sufficient to activate Mamo in young/maturing MB neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: chinmo-RNAi effectively reduced Chinmo levels early in development, so that immunostaining at 48 hr ALH reveals very low levels, both in newborn neurons and in older, early-born neurons.
source: chinmo-RNAi effectively reduced Chinmo levels early in development, so that immunostaining at 48 hr ALH reveals very low levels, both in newborn neurons and in older, early-born neurons (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1B and G.

claim: The initiation of Mamo expression is only shifted as early as 60 hr ALH with chinmo-RNAi.
source: Nevertheless, the initiation of Mamo expression is only shifted as early as 60 hr ALH (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B, Figure 3—figure supplement 2A and B.

claim: The timing of early Mamo expression with chinmo-RNAi correlates with the onset of Syp expression.
source: This timing correlates with the onset of Syp expression (Liu et al., 2015), making us wonder whether Mamo could also be regulated by upstream temporal factor Syp.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and represents an inference from the data.

claim: Repressing Syp increased Chinmo expression.
source: Repressing Syp increased Chinmo expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G) and thus abolished Mamo expression at 84 hr ALH (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G, and Figure 3B.

claim: Repressing Syp abolished Mamo expression at 84 hr ALH.
source: Repressing Syp increased Chinmo expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and G) and thus abolished Mamo expression at 84 hr ALH (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3B.

claim: Ectopic Syp marginally reduced Chinmo levels.
source: Ectopic Syp marginally reduced Chinmo levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) and there was a concomitant shift in Mamo expression—like chinmo-RNAi, there was an increased number of Mamo-positive cells at 84 hr ALH (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3—figure supplement 1F and Figure 3C.

claim: Ectopic Syp resulted in an increased number of Mamo-positive cells at 84 hr ALH.
source: Ectopic Syp marginally reduced Chinmo levels (Figure 3—figure supplement 1F) and there was a concomitant shift in Mamo expression—like chinmo-RNAi, there was an increased number of Mamo-positive cells at 84 hr ALH (Figure 3C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3C.

claim: Without Syp, weak Chinmo was no longer sufficient to promote Mamo expression.
source: Intriguingly in this scenario, Mamo was still absent (Figure 3D). Without Syp, weak Chinmo was no longer sufficient to promote Mamo expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3D.

claim: mamo is transcriptionally controlled by weak Chinmo but post-transcriptionally regulated by the Syp RNA-binding protein.
source: It is therefore possible that mamo is transcriptionally controlled by weak Chinmo but post-transcriptionally regulated by the Syp RNA-binding protein.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis based on the experimental observations.

claim: An onset of mamo transcription in the nuclei of newborn mushroom body neurons starts at 72 hr ALH.
source: We detected an onset of mamo transcription in the nuclei of newborn MB neurons starting at 72 hr ALH (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4D showing smFISH data.

claim: Mature mamo transcripts gradually accumulated in the cytoplasm of young/maturing neurons.
source: Mature mamo transcripts then gradually accumulated in the cytoplasm of young/maturing neurons (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4E showing smFISH data.

claim: Knocking down Chinmo by targeted RNAi elicited a precocious activation of mamo transcription as early as 48 hr ALH.
source: Consistent with our previous results, knocking down Chinmo by targeted RNAi elicited a precocious activation of mamo transcription as early as 48 hr ALH (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4F showing smFISH data.

claim: Repressing Syp did not delay the precocious induction of mamo transcription due to chinmo-RNAi.
source: When examining MBs lacking Syp that also had very weak Chinmo expression (Syp-RNAi + chinmo-RNAi, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and I), we found sites of active mamo transcription at 48 hr ALH (Figure 4I). This clearly illustrates that repressing Syp did not delay the precocious induction of mamo transcription due to chinmo-RNAi.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4I and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E and I.

claim: Loss of Syp blocked the accumulation of mature mamo transcripts.
source: Instead, loss of Syp blocked the accumulation of mature mamo transcripts (Figure 4I–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4I-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Without Syp the active sites of mamo transcription were short-lived, never surviving beyond the newborn neuron stage.
source: Meanwhile, without Syp the active sites of mamo transcription were short-lived, never surviving beyond the newborn neuron stage (Figure 4I–K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4I-K and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Syp is required post-transcriptionally for mamo mRNA maturation and sustained mamo transcription.
source: These observations indicate that Syp is required post-transcriptionally for mamo mRNA maturation and sustained mamo transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the smFISH data.

claim: Transcriptional maintenance of mamo may be due to positive feedback by the Mamo protein itself.
source: This transcriptional maintenance may be due to positive feedback by the Mamo protein itself.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a hypothesis.

claim: mamo-RNAi did not inhibit mamo induction in newborn neurons.
source: Consistent with this notion, mamo-RNAi did not inhibit mamo induction in newborn neurons (Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but prevented mamo mRNA maturation and sustained mamo transcription (Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: mamo-RNAi prevented mamo mRNA maturation and sustained mamo transcription.
source: Consistent with this notion, mamo-RNAi did not inhibit mamo induction in newborn neurons (Figure 4L and Figure 4—figure supplement 1), but prevented mamo mRNA maturation and sustained mamo transcription (Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 4M and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: mamo-RNAi caused the α'/β' lobes to essentially vanish.
source: In keeping with our hypothesis, mamo-RNAi caused the α'/β' lobes to essentially vanish (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C.

claim: Wildtype α'/β' cell bodies characteristically express strong Trio, both in the cytoplasm and plasma membrane.
source: Wildtype α'/β' cell bodies characteristically express strong Trio, both in the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Awasaki et al., 2000) (Figure 5B and B'), whereas we detected little to no Trio expression in MB neurons expressing mamo-RNAi (Figure 5C').
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and supported by Figure 5B and B'.

claim: Little to no Trio expression was detected in mushroom body neurons expressing mamo-RNAi.
source: Wildtype α'/β' cell bodies characteristically express strong Trio, both in the cytoplasm and plasma membrane (Awasaki et al., 2000) (Figure 5B and B'), whereas we detected little to no Trio expression in MB neurons expressing mamo-RNAi (Figure 5C').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C'.

claim: Mamo has a significant role in proper α'/β' fate specification.
source: This demonstrates a significant role for Mamo in proper α'/β' fate specification.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The number of cells expressing the γ-specific marker, Abrupt, is reduced with mamo-RNAi.
source: Nevertheless, Mamo may be pleiotropic, as the number of cells expressing the γ-specific marker, Abrupt, is also reduced (Figure 5C').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C'.

claim: With premature weak Chinmo (chinmo-RNAi), γ neuron production significantly decreased from 38 ± 0.3% in control animals to 18 ± 1.6% with chinmo-RNAi.
source: With premature weak Chinmo (chinmo-RNAi), γ neuron production significantly (p<0.001) decreased from 38 ± 0.3% in control animals to 18 ± 1.6% with chinmo-RNAi (Figure 5D and D' and Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5D and D' and Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: With chinmo-RNAi, the window of α'/β' production was shifted earlier, rather than prolonged.
source: This suggests an early onset of α'/β' neuron production and is consistent with the early Mamo transcription initiation at 48 hr ALH (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1) and early Mamo expression at 60 hr ALH (Figure 2F) that we detected with chinmo-RNAi. However, the percentage of α'/β' cells did not significantly increase. This suggests that with chinmo-RNAi, the window of α'/β' production was shifted earlier, rather than prolonged.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: The percentage of α/β-characteristic Trio-/Abrupt- cells increased from 41 ± 0.5% in control to 64 ± 1.1% with chinmo-RNAi.
source: The percentage of α/β-characteristic Trio-/Abrupt- cells increased from 41 ± 0.5% in control to 64 ± 1.1% with chinmo-RNAi (p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents quantified data.

claim: The combination of mamo-RNAi and chinmo-RNAi completely eliminated α'/β' neuronal features.
source: Strikingly, the combination of mamo-RNAi and chinmo-RNAi completely eliminated α'/β' neuronal features (Figure 5E and E').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5E and E'.

claim: Mamo has an essential role in α'/β' temporal fate determination.
source: This result substantiates an essential role for Mamo in α'/β' temporal fate determination.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: The mamo gene has seven splice isoforms that produce four protein variants.
source: The mamo gene has seven splice isoforms that produce four protein variants (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1A and B.

claim: Only the Mamo variant with four zinc fingers produced mushroom bodies that were not reduced in size, but had reduced Fas-II labeling.
source: We tested the three variants containing zinc fingers (codon optimized and lacking UTRs and introns) and found that only the Mamo variant with four zinc fingers (4ZF: corresponding to mamo isoforms RG and RF) produced MBs that were not reduced in size, but had reduced Fas-II labeling (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C–F), reminiscent of a shift in temporal fate specification.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1C-F.

claim: The 4ZF Mamo construct could override the mamo-RNAi phenotype.
source: Importantly, we confirmed that the 4ZF Mamo construct could override the mamo-RNAi phenotype (Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 1G and H.

claim: Either the mamo-RF or mamo-RG isoform lies downstream of Imp/Syp gradients and Chinmo in α'/β' temporal fate determination.
source: These data strongly indicate that either the mamo-RF or mamo-RG isoform lies downstream of Imp/Syp gradients and Chinmo in α'/β' temporal fate determination.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: 4ZF Mamo overexpression does not alter Imp, Syp or Chinmo levels.
source: In further support of a hierarchy, 4ZF Mamo overexpression does not alter Imp, Syp or Chinmo levels (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Continuous expression of transgenic Mamo greatly enlarged the α'/β' lobes and drastically reduced the thickness of the α/β lobes.
source: Continuous expression of transgenic Mamo greatly enlarged the α'/β' lobes and drastically reduced the thickness of the α/β lobes (Figure 5F), as determined by Trio and Fas-II expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5F.

claim: The reciprocal changes in Trio and Fas-II expression with Mamo overexpression indicate an extension of α'/β' production into the pupal stage.
source: The reciprocal changes in Trio and Fas-II expression indicate an extension of α'/β' production into the pupal stage, when wildtype MB NBs produce α/β neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an interpretation of the data.

claim: The percentage of α'/β'-characteristic TrioPM,Cyto expressing cells increased from 20 ± 0.8% in control to 32 ± 1.8% with mamo-GOF.
source: The percentage of α'/β'-characteristic TrioPM,Cyto expressing cells increased from 20 ± 0.8% in control to 32 ± 1.8% with mamo-GOF (p<0.005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents quantified data.

claim: The percentage of α/β-characteristic Trio- expressing cells decreased from 41 ± 0.5% in control to 2 ± 0.4% with mamo-GOF.
source: The percentage of α/β-characteristic Trio- expressing cells decreased from 41 ± 0.5% in control to 2 ± 0.4% with mamo-GOF (p<0.001).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and represents quantified data.

claim: With Syp-RNAi, neuroblasts do not appear to age.
source: As previously reported (Yang et al., 2017), the Syp-RNAi expressing NBs cycled incessantly (Figure 5G, NBs marked with asterisks).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation and supported by Figure 5G.

claim: With Syp-RNAi, temporal progression stalled, producing only γ neurons.
source: Moreover, temporal progression stalled, producing only γ neurons, as determined by both lobe morphology and marker expression (Figure 5G and G').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5G and G'.

claim: The addition of transgenic Mamo to Syp-RNAi caused the majority of neurons to assume the α'/β' fate.
source: The addition of transgenic Mamo caused the majority of neurons to assume the α'/β' fate (Figure 5H and H').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5H and H'.

claim: Mamo overexpression did not alter the continued neuroblast division.
source: Note that Mamo overexpression did not alter the continued NB division (Figure 5H', asterisks).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5H'.

claim: Mamo is both necessary and sufficient to determine the middle α'/β' temporal fate.
source: These results confirm that Mamo is both necessary and sufficient to determine the middle α'/β' temporal fate.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Mamo acts as a key temporal fate determinant for the α'/β' neuronal fate in the serial temporal fate diversification of mushroom body neurons.
source: Taken together, our findings indicate that Mamo acts as a key temporal fate determinant for the α'/β' neuronal fate in the serial temporal fate diversification of MB neurons.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Mamo continues to be expressed in adult α'/β' neurons.
source: As Mamo is essential for α'/β' neuronal fate specification and continues to be expressed in adult α'/β' neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), we wanted to examine whether it is required to maintain α'/β' cell fate.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Expression of mamo-RNAi for 21 days after adult eclosion was required to effectively reduce Mamo protein levels.
source: After adult eclosion, expression of mamo-RNAi for 21 days was required to effectively reduce Mamo protein levels (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: When Mamo was efficiently knocked down in adult mushroom bodies, the α'/β'-characteristic cytoplasmic Trio was completely absent.
source: When Mamo was efficiently knocked down in adult MBs, the α'/β'-characteristic cytoplasmic Trio (TrioCyto,PM/Abrupt-) was completely absent (Figure 6C and C', 22 ± 1.6% control vs 0 ± 0% mamo-RNAi, p<0.0005).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6C and C'.

claim: Mamo is required to maintain α'/β' cell-type specific Trio expression.
source: These results clearly demonstrate that Mamo is required to maintain α'/β' cell-type specific Trio expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Overexpressing Mamo in adult mushroom body neurons resulted in a modest, but significant increase in the percentage of cells with α'/β' characteristic gene expression.
source: Overexpressing Mamo in adult MB neurons resulted in a modest, but significant increase in the percentage of cells with α'/β' characteristic gene expression (TrioPM,Cyto/Abrupt-, 22 ± 1.6% control vs 42 ± 4.1% Mamo-GOF, p=0.01; Figure 6D and D').
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6D and D'.

claim: The ability of Mamo overexpression to transform mushroom body neurons diminished over time.
source: Markedly, the ability of Mamo overexpression to transform MB neurons diminished over time, as transgene induction at pupal development was more effective at increasing TrioPM,Cyto/Abrupt- cells (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Mamo acts as a terminal selector transcription factor for α'/β' neuronal fate, in part by regulating Trio gene expression.
source: Taken together, our data suggests that Mamo acts as a terminal selector transcription factor for α'/β' neuronal fate, in part by regulating Trio gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Imp and Syp temporal protein gradients show distinct lineage-characteristic expression levels and rates of gradient progression.
source: Interestingly, Imp and Syp temporal protein gradients show distinct lineage-characteristic expression levels and rates of gradient progression (Liu et al., 2015; Ren et al., 2017; Syed et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mushroom body neuroblasts have shallow, slowly progressing gradients.
source: MB NBs have shallow, slowly progressing gradients and AL NBs have steep, rapidly progressing gradients (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Antennal lobe neuroblasts have steep, rapidly progressing gradients.
source: MB NBs have shallow, slowly progressing gradients and AL NBs have steep, rapidly progressing gradients (Liu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mamo expression was found in at least two of the four labeled antennal lobe lineages at 84 hr ALH.
source: We found Mamo expression in at least two of the four labeled AL lineages at 84 hr ALH (Figure 7D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7D.

claim: Weak Chinmo (chinmo-RNAi) induced precocious Mamo expression in antennal lobe lineages.
source: Similar to our findings in the MB, weak Chinmo (chinmo-RNAi) induced precocious Mamo expression (Figure 7B) and an increase in the number of Mamo-positive neurons at 84 hr ALH (Figure 7F).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7B and 7F.

claim: Mamo expression was lost when Syp was repressed in antennal lobe lineages.
source: Moreover, Mamo expression was lost when Syp was repressed (Figure 7C and G).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7C and G.

claim: Weak Chinmo and Syp specifically guide Mamo expression in defined temporal windows of diverse lineages.
source: These findings in the AL combined with our previous MB data leads us to a model where weak Chinmo and Syp specifically guide Mamo expression in defined temporal windows of diverse lineages (Figure 8).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the experimental data and supported by Figure 8.

claim: ChIP-chip performed in embryos found five Chinmo binding sites within the mamo gene.
source: ChIP-chip performed in embryos found five Chinmo binding sites within the mamo gene (Roy et al., 2010), consistent with direct activation of mamo transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: ChIP-chip data is consistent with direct activation of mamo transcription by Chinmo.
source: ChIP-chip performed in embryos found five Chinmo binding sites within the mamo gene (Roy et al., 2010), consistent with direct activation of mamo transcription.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from cited data.

claim: In the testis, Chinmo is suspected to function as a transcriptional repressor.
source: However, in the testis, Chinmo is suspected to function as a transcriptional repressor (Flaherty et al., 2010; Grmai et al., 2018).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Mamo expression is positively autoregulated.
source: Given our finding that Mamo expression is positively autoregulated (Figure 4L and M) and that Mamo continues to be expressed into adult neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1C), it is particularly important to control the timing of Mamo's onset.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 4L and M.

claim: SYNCRIP is involved with multiple facets of mRNA regulation including mRNA splicing and maturation.
source: SYNCRIP is involved with multiple facets of mRNA regulation including mRNA splicing and maturation (Mourelatos et al., 2001), mRNA localization and stabilization (Bannai et al., 2004) as well as inhibiting mRNA translation and miRNA-mediated repression via competition with Poly(A) binding proteins (Svitkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: SYNCRIP is involved with mRNA localization and stabilization.
source: SYNCRIP is involved with multiple facets of mRNA regulation including mRNA splicing and maturation (Mourelatos et al., 2001), mRNA localization and stabilization (Bannai et al., 2004) as well as inhibiting mRNA translation and miRNA-mediated repression via competition with Poly(A) binding proteins (Svitkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: SYNCRIP inhibits mRNA translation and miRNA-mediated repression via competition with Poly(A) binding proteins.
source: SYNCRIP is involved with multiple facets of mRNA regulation including mRNA splicing and maturation (Mourelatos et al., 2001), mRNA localization and stabilization (Bannai et al., 2004) as well as inhibiting mRNA translation and miRNA-mediated repression via competition with Poly(A) binding proteins (Svitkin et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Drosophila Syp was isolated from the spliceosome B complex, indicating a conserved role in mRNA splicing.
source: Drosophila Syp was isolated from the spliceosome B complex, indicating a conserved role in mRNA splicing (Herold et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Syp has roles in mRNA localization and stabilization.
source: Syp has likewise been found to operate in mRNA localization and stabilization (McDermott et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Syp has clear roles in altering protein expression of its mRNA targets, both positively and negatively.
source: Furthermore, it has clear roles in altering protein expression of its mRNA targets, both positively and negatively (McDermott et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Syp directly binds mamo mRNA and aids in its splicing, maturation and/or stabilization.
source: In the absence of Syp, mamo transcription was initiated prematurely in response to weak Chinmo levels, yet mature transcripts failed to accumulate (Figure 4L–K). This leads us to believe that Syp directly binds mamo mRNA and aids in its splicing, maturation and/or stabilization.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as an inference from the experimental data.

claim: Overexpressing a mamo cDNA (lacking 5' UTR, 3' UTR and introns) was able to promote cell fate changes despite repression of Syp.
source: This is consistent with our finding that overexpressing a mamo cDNA (lacking 5' UTR, 3' UTR and introns) was able to promote cell fate changes despite repression of Syp (Figure 5H).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion and supported by Figure 5H.

claim: Chinmo is required for EcR-B1 expression.
source: As in our first Chinmo study (Zhu et al., 2006), Marchetti and Tavosanis demonstrate that Chinmo is required for EcR-B1 expression; however it remains unclear whether Chinmo directly affects EcR-B1 expression or if the Chinmo-dependent EcR-B1 expression is the sole mechanism for γ neuron temporal fate specification.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ecdysone receptor signaling has known effects on mushroom body cell morphology.
source: Moreover, neuronal temporal fate is not accurately determined by neuronal morphology alone, particularly when ecdysone signaling has known effects on MB cell morphology (Lee et al., 2000) and fate (Kucherenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ecdysone receptor signaling has known effects on mushroom body cell fate.
source: Moreover, neuronal temporal fate is not accurately determined by neuronal morphology alone, particularly when ecdysone signaling has known effects on MB cell morphology (Lee et al., 2000) and fate (Kucherenko et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ecdysone receptor signaling is highly pleiotropic.
source: Ecdysone receptor signaling is highly pleiotropic (Alyagor et al., 2018), including ligand-independent functions (Mouillet et al., 2001) making dominant-negative and overexpression studies difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Ecdysone receptor has ligand-independent functions.
source: Ecdysone receptor signaling is highly pleiotropic (Alyagor et al., 2018), including ligand-independent functions (Mouillet et al., 2001) making dominant-negative and overexpression studies difficult to interpret.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: Chinmo functions in newborn neurons to promote temporal fate as weak Chinmo expression directly precedes Mamo transcription.
source: This current manuscript strongly promotes the idea that Chinmo functions in newborn neurons to promote temporal fate as weak Chinmo expression (Figure 3—figure supplement 1) directly precedes Mamo transcription (Figure 4) and Mamo is essential for specification (Figure 5) and maintenance of α'/β' fate (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the experimental data.

claim: Analogous mechanisms to the multilayered hierarchical system described likely underlie temporal patterning in mammalian brains.
source: We describe a multilayered hierarchical system to define distinct neuronal temporal fate that culminates in the expression of a terminal selector gene. Analogous mechanisms likely underlie temporal patterning in mammalian brains.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a speculation based on the findings.

claim: Both Imp and Syp homologs are highly expressed in the developing mouse brain and play vital roles in neural development and/or neuronal morphology.
source: Both homologs are highly expressed in the developing mouse brain and play vital roles in neural development and/or neuronal morphology (Chen et al., 2012; Mori et al., 2001; Perycz et al., 2011; Williams et al., 2016; Xing et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The opposing functions of Imp and Syp appear to be conserved, as the murine orthologs IMP1 and SYNCRIP bind the identical RNA to either promote or repress axon growth, respectively.
source: The opposing functions of Imp and Syp also appear to be conserved, as the murine orthologs IMP1 and SYNCRIP bind the identical RNA to either promote (Donnelly et al., 2013) or repress axon growth (Williams et al., 2016), respectively.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: IMP1 expression in fetal mouse neural stem cells plays important roles in stem cell maintenance and proper temporal progression of neurogenesis.
source: Moreover, IMP1 expression in fetal mouse neural stem cells plays important roles in stem cell maintenance and proper temporal progression of neurogenesis.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on established knowledge.

claim: Chinmo and Mamo are both BTB-ZF (broad-complex, tram-track and bric-à-brac - zinc finger) transcription factors.
source: While Chinmo and Mamo have no clear mammalian orthologs, they are both BTB-ZF (broad-complex, tram-track and bric-à-brac - zinc finger) transcription factors (Mukai et al., 2007; Zhu et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The BTB domain is a protein interaction domain that can form homo or heterodimers and also binds transcriptional regulators such as repressors, activators and chromatin remodelers.
source: The BTB domain is a protein interaction domain that can form homo or heterodimers and also binds transcriptional regulators such as repressors, activators and chromatin remodelers (Perez-Torrado et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: The C2H2 (Krüppel-like) zinc fingers bind DNA—providing target specificity.
source: The C2H2 (Krüppel-like) zinc fingers bind DNA—providing target specificity.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on established knowledge.

claim: BTB-ZF proteins have been found to be critical regulators of developmental processes, including neural development.
source: BTB-ZF proteins have been found to be critical regulators of developmental processes, including neural development (Chaharbakhshi and Jemc, 2016; Siggs and Beutler, 2012).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: The BTB-zinc finger protein, Zbtb20, appears to be essential for early-to-late neuronal identity in the mouse cortex.
source: Indeed, the BTB-zinc finger protein, Zbtb20, appears to be essential for early-to-late neuronal identity in the mouse cortex (Tonchev et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Zbtb20 is temporally expressed in cortical progenitors and knockout results in cortical layering defects.
source: Zbtb20 is temporally expressed in cortical progenitors and knockout results in cortical layering defects (Tonchev et al., 2016), as the inside-out layering of the cortex follows neuronal birth order.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with a citation to support the claim.

claim: Mutations of other brain-expressed BTB-ZF proteins show cortical layering phenotypes.
source: While mutations of other brain-expressed BTB-ZF proteins also show cortical layering phenotypes (Carter et al., 2000; Okado et al., 2009), potential roles in temporal patterning have not been explored.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citations to support the claim.

claim: A layered series of temporal protein gradients guide the expression of terminal selector genes in the fate specification process described.
source: In this study, we illustrate a fate specification process in which a layered series of temporal protein gradients guide the expression of terminal selector genes.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: The first-tier temporal gradients are expressed in neural stem cells, followed by a restricted expression window in newborn neurons to finally induce a terminal selector gene in a subset of neurons as they mature.
source: The first-tier temporal gradients are expressed in neural stem cells, followed by a restricted expression window in newborn neurons to finally induce a terminal selector gene in a subset of neurons as they mature.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Mamo may serve as a temporally defined, terminal selector gene in a variety of lineages in the Drosophila brain.
source: Corresponding data in the AL lineages suggest that Mamo may serve as a temporally defined, terminal selector gene in a variety of lineages in the Drosophila brain.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as an inference from the study's findings.

claim: Multi-tiered, bimodal regulation ensures that only the progeny in a precise temporal window (those with both weak Chinmo and significant Syp levels) can effectively activate the terminal selector gene, mamo.
source: This multi-tiered, bimodal regulation ensures that only the progeny in a precise temporal window (those with both weak Chinmo and significant Syp levels) can effectively activate the terminal selector gene, mamo.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as a summary of the study's findings.

claim: Utilizing layers of temporal gradients to define discrete temporal windows mirrors how in early embryos the spatial gradients of RNA-binding proteins and transcription factors specify the fly's A/P axis.
source: This discovery attests to the power of gradients in creating diverse cells from a single progenitor. Utilizing layers of temporal gradients to define discrete temporal windows mirrors how in early embryos the spatial gradients of RNA-binding proteins and transcription factors specify the fly's A/P axis.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as an analogy to support the findings.

claim: The paradigm described provides considerable complexity of gene network regulation, leading to abundant neural cell diversity.
source: This paradigm provides considerable complexity of gene network regulation, leading to abundant neural cell diversity.
evidence: This is stated in the conclusions as a summary of the study's implications.
